<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and were disciplined with evidence. PRO's opening framed the stakes vividly ("transfer of high ground," "title should not move first") and its "feeding the choke" argument was a real answer to CON's starvation claim. But CON's pressure questions did decisive work: Q1 forced PRO to name concrete rebuttal showings (irrevocable allied offtake, audited capital stack, personnel restrictions), and CON immediately reframed these as exactly the mitigation conditions targeted review imposes, collapsing the difference between the rules to "the default when disclosure is partial" — then in closing noted that conditioned review also refuses to close until conditions are met, so PRO's "capture" is a bad reviewer, not a bad rule. Q2 extracted PRO's concession that a decade of undeveloped deposit is "a commercial cost," which CON turned against PRO's own metric (material commandable when a crisis starts; idle rock cannot be commanded). PRO's replies largely repeated "rock cannot arm a ship without a mill" and "idle rock is an option" without answering CON's mechanism that flowing feedstock is what makes allied mills bankable, nor CON's point that PRO's own definition of "closely tied" (export-license dependence) sweeps in ordinary producers. CON's clipped Rebuttal 2 was a minor execution cost, but it had already delivered its A1/A2 and weighing. CON made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A2/[A4.3]-[A4.6]: after PRO listed the buyer's required showings in [B4.1], CON argued PRO had just described mitigation, erasing the "reviewer cannot see" objection and leaving only a dispute over defaults — paired with PRO's "commercial cost" concession, CON framed the presumption as paying a decade of lost supply for what conditions already achieve. PRO's "that default is the capture" response was sharp but did not survive CON's closing point that conditioned review also doesn't close on a partial file.</best_rebuttal>
